html:
The first telegraph cables laid across the floor of the Atlantic Ocean, from Valentia Island in Ireland to Newfoundland, between 1858 and 1866. They cut the time for news to cross between Europe and America from about ten days by ship to minutes.

The American businessman Cyrus West Field led the Atlantic Telegraph Company. The first cable worked in August 1858: Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchanged messages, and New York held celebrations. Within weeks it failed, partly because too high a voltage was used. A second attempt in 1865 broke at sea.

In 1866 the giant steamship Great Eastern laid a new cable that worked, then found and finished the lost 1865 cable. The physicist William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, made the science of signalling through long cables work. Markets, newspapers and governments on both sides now shared news on the same day. Within decades cables circled the globe, from the telegraph network of Europe to Australia's Overland Telegraph Line.
